title: The nuclear model of the atom
examTip: When describing Rutherford's experiment, link each observation to its conclusion. Most go straight through: the atom is mostly empty space. Some are deflected: the positive nucleus repels them. Very few bounce back: the nucleus is small and dense. Each observation needs its own explanation for full marks.
introTips: Scientists in 1900 didn't know atoms had a nucleus at all. They thought positive charge was spread evenly throughout.
Rutherford's experiment was one of the most surprising in physics. He said it was as shocking as firing a shell at tissue paper and having it bounce back.
The nuclear model we use today was built on Rutherford's work. It took decades to refine.
Proton number (atomic number) tells you the element. Mass number tells you the total number of protons and neutrons.
Electrons sit in shells at fixed energy levels. This explains how atoms behave in chemistry and how they give out light.
intro: How do you find out what is inside something you cannot see? That was the challenge facing physicists in the early 1900s. They fired tiny particles at atoms and watched where they went. This led to one of the most important discoveries in science: the nucleus. This story is not just history. It shows how evidence forces scientists to drop a comfortable model and replace it with a better one. The nuclear model it produced explains chemical reactions, radioactive decay and even the power of the Sun.

keyPoints.heading: Thomson's plum pudding model
keyPoints.content: Before Rutherford, the best model of the atom was Thomson's plum pudding model (1904). J.J. Thomson had already discovered the electron (1897). This is a tiny, negatively charged particle. He suggested that the atom was a sphere of diffuse positive charge, with electrons embedded throughout it. It was like plums in a pudding. The atom was neutral overall, because the negative electrons balanced the spread-out positive charge. This model predicted what would happen if you fired particles at atoms. They would all pass straight through, with very slight deflections. The positive charge was too spread out to cause big deflections. This prediction turned out to be almost completely wrong. That is what made Rutherford's results so dramatic.
writeBullets: Thomson's plum pudding model — the atom is a sphere of diffuse positive charge with electrons embedded in it
Thomson discovered the electron in 1897. It is a tiny, negatively charged particle
The model predicted that fired particles would pass straight through, with only tiny deflections
The atom is neutral overall. The negative electrons balance the spread-out positive charge
Rutherford's gold foil experiment disproved this model

keyTerms.def: Thomson's model: a sphere of diffuse positive charge with electrons embedded throughout, like plums in a pudding
A tiny, negatively charged particle in the atom; discovered by Thomson in 1897

keyPoints.memTip: Plum pudding = positive 'dough' with electron 'plums' dotted through it. It was replaced by Rutherford's nuclear model.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Be able to contrast the plum pudding prediction (all particles go through) with what Rutherford really found.

keyPoints.heading: Rutherford's gold foil experiment
keyPoints.content: In 1909, Geiger and Marsden worked with Rutherford. They fired a beam of alpha particles at an extremely thin sheet of gold foil. Alpha particles are positively charged and came from a radioactive source. A screen that flashed when hit showed where the particles went. There were three key observations, each with a conclusion. (1) Most alpha particles went straight through → the atom is mostly empty space. The positive charge is not spread out as the plum pudding model said. (2) Some alpha particles were deflected at small angles → there is a small, dense, positively charged region at the centre. It repels some alpha particles. (3) A very small number bounced almost straight back → the positive charge is packed into an extremely small, dense nucleus. Only direct hits cause the large deflections. This was called the nuclear model.
writeBullets: Alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil. A detector screen recorded where they went
Most went straight through → atom is mostly empty space
Some deflected at small angles → a small, dense, positive nucleus repels alpha particles
Very few bounced almost back → nucleus is tiny and highly concentrated
Result: the plum pudding model was dropped, and the nuclear model was proposed

keyTerms.def: Rutherford's 1909 experiment: alpha particles fired at gold foil; results showed atoms have a tiny, dense, positive nucleus
Atomic model proposed by Rutherford: tiny, dense, positive nucleus at the centre with electrons orbiting in empty space
A particle consisting of 2 protons + 2 neutrons; positively charged; used as the 'probe' in Rutherford's experiment

keyPoints.memTip: Most through = empty space. Some deflect = positive nucleus repels.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Exam questions often ask 'what does observation X tell us about the structure of the atom?'. Link each result directly to a conclusion about structure.

keyPoints.heading: Structure of the nucleus — protons, neutrons and electrons
keyPoints.content: The nuclear model gives us the structure of the atom. There is a tiny, dense, positive nucleus at the centre. It is surrounded by electrons in shells. Almost all of the atom is empty space. The nucleus contains: - protons (positive charge, relative mass 1) - neutrons (no charge, relative mass 1) Electrons orbit in shells (relative charge −1, relative mass ~1/1836 ≈ essentially 0). Key numbers: - Atomic number (proton number, Z) = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom. It decides the element. - Mass number (A) = number of protons + number of neutrons. - Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Example: carbon-12 has atomic number 6 → 6 protons, 6 electrons. Its mass number is 12 → 12 − 6 = 6 neutrons.
writeBullets: Nucleus — tiny, dense and positive. Contains protons and neutrons
Proton — relative charge +1, relative mass 1
Neutron — relative charge 0, relative mass 1
Electron — relative charge −1, relative mass ~0 (negligible). In shells around the nucleus
Atomic number (Z) = number of protons = number of electrons (neutral atom)
Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons. Neutrons = A − Z

keyTerms.def: The number of protons in the nucleus; determines which element the atom is
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
A neutral particle in the nucleus; relative mass 1, relative charge 0

keyPoints.memTip: A = protons + neutrons. Z = protons only.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Practise reading isotope notation like ²³⁸₉₂U. The top number is the mass number. The bottom is the atomic number.

keyPoints.heading: Electron shells and energy levels
keyPoints.content: Electrons do not orbit randomly. They sit in shells at fixed distances from the nucleus. Each shell matches a fixed energy level. The innermost shell (lowest energy) fills first, then the next, and so on. Electrons can absorb energy to jump to a higher energy level, further from the nucleus. They become 'excited'. When they fall back to a lower level, they emit electromagnetic radiation (light) of a specific frequency. This is why each element gives a unique spectrum. Bohr refined this model further (1913). At GCSE, you need to know three things. Electrons are in shells. Shells stand for energy levels. Moving between shells means absorbing or emitting radiation.
writeBullets: Electrons occupy shells at fixed energy levels around the nucleus
The innermost shell has the lowest energy and fills first
Absorb energy → the electron jumps to a higher energy level (excited state)
Fall back to a lower level → emit electromagnetic radiation of a specific frequency

keyTerms.def: A fixed energy level around the nucleus where electrons reside; inner shells fill first
A fixed amount of energy associated with each electron shell; electrons can jump between levels by absorbing or emitting radiation

keyPoints.memTip: Shells = energy levels. Jump up = absorb energy.
keyPoints.tutor_note: At GCSE, you just need to know two things. Electrons are in shells at set energy levels. Moving between them emits radiation.

tables.title: Rutherford's gold foil — observations and conclusions
rows: Most alpha particles passed straight through
Some alpha particles deflected at small angles
Small, positively charged nucleus repels alpha particles
A very few bounced almost straight back
Nucleus is tiny, dense and contains almost all the atom's mass

0.question: In Thomson's plum pudding model, where was the positive charge in an atom?
options: Spread evenly through a diffuse sphere, with electrons embedded in it
Concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus at the centre
Only in the electrons, which carried both positive and negative charges
In a ring around the outside of the atom
0.correctFeedback: Correct! In the plum pudding model, positive charge was spread through the atom like a pudding. Electrons ('plums') were dotted through it.
0.wrongFeedback: The plum pudding model pictured positive charge spread evenly through the whole atom, not in a central nucleus. The nucleus idea came later, from Rutherford's experiment.

1.question: In Rutherford's experiment, a very small number of alpha particles bounced almost straight back. What does this tell us?
options: The nucleus is very small and dense, with a large positive charge packed into it
The atom is mostly empty space with no charge
Alpha particles are negatively charged and attracted to the centre
The gold foil was too thick for most particles to pass through
1.correctFeedback: Exactly right! Only a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus could send an alpha particle back. A spread-out charge would not repel it that strongly.
1.wrongFeedback: Large deflections (bouncing back) need a large force. Only a packed, dense positive charge can give that. This showed the nucleus is tiny but holds almost all the positive charge.

2.question: An atom has an atomic number of 8 and a mass number of 18. How many neutrons does it have?
2.correctFeedback: Correct! Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 18 − 8 = 10.
2.wrongFeedback: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 18 − 8 = 10. The atomic number counts protons only. Subtract it from the mass number to find neutrons.

3.question: An atom has 2 electrons in its first shell and 7 in its second. How many electrons does it have in total? Which period of the periodic table is it in?
3.correctFeedback: Correct. 2 + 7 = 9 electrons in total. The first shell holds up to 2 electrons, and the second holds up to 8. The outer electrons are in the second shell, so this is a Period 2 element. It happens to be fluorine.
3.wrongFeedback: Count the electrons: 2 (first shell) + 7 (second shell) = 9 total. The period number tells you how many electron shells are in use. Two shells filled = Period 2. The first shell fills at 2; the second fills at 8.

commonMistakes: Saying 'the atom is mostly empty space' without linking it to the Rutherford experiment. Link it to the fact that most alpha particles went straight through.
Mixing up mass number and atomic number. Atomic number is protons only (bottom number). Mass number is protons + neutrons (top number).
Saying electrons are 'in the nucleus'. They orbit the nucleus in shells. Only protons and neutrons are in the nucleus.
Describing Rutherford's experiment as 'light fired at gold'. It used alpha particles (positively charged helium nuclei), not light.
Forgetting that a neutral atom has the same number of electrons as protons. That number equals the atomic number.
examTips: For the gold foil experiment, always give three separate observations. Match each one to a conclusion about structure. Usually there is one mark per observation and conclusion pair.
To find the number of neutrons: neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Write this formula down before calculating.
Compare the plum pudding model and the nuclear model. The key difference is where the positive charge is. It is spread out in one, and packed into a tiny nucleus in the other.
If asked why the plum pudding model was dropped, say what it failed to predict. It did not predict the large-angle deflections and backscattering of alpha particles.
